Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We have carefully reviewed the cited literature, which primarily focuses on metal fabrication on polymer substrates and patterning of liquid metals via metallic templates. The knowledge from these studies can indeed be conceptually transferred to the patterned fabrication of liquid metals. However, our work is situated within the distinct field of fiber electronics. Although liquid metals have been widely studied, a method for their liquid-phase fabrication at the single-fiber level has not been reported. Notably, the adaptation of thin-film electronic techniques to single-fiber devices is significant enough to warrant publication in high-impact journals, including those in the Nature family, highlighting a key opportunity for innovation that our work aims to address. For instance, single-fiber electroluminescent devices have been reported (Nature Photon. 9, 233–238, 2015), even though flexible electroluminescent devices have already been widely studied. Similarly, single-fiber batteries have recently been demonstrated (Nature 629, 86–91, 2024), despite the extensive prior development of flexible battery technologies.
In terms of specific innovations in fabrication, current liquid metal fiber production methods primarily rely on directly coating or injecting liquid metal into hollow or thermoplastic fibers to form LM-core structures (Liquid Metal Fibers, Adv. Fiber Mater. 4, 987–1004, 2022). These approaches often suffer from uneven coating, relatively large diameters, or poor skin contact of the conductive components. Our study addresses these challenges by introducing a liquid-phase processing strategy for the fabrication of single LM fibers. Unlike large-area thin films or woven fabrics, the processing of individual fibers is inherently more complex. At the microscale, highly uniform electrochemical deposition is required to achieve continuous and stable LM fiber formation. In the revised manuscript, we have further investigated the influence of various fabrication parameters on LM deposition and fiber quality. Moreover, beyond the chemical deposition of LM fibers, we have seamlessly integrated inert electrodes to develop an LM-fiber-based conductive sensing system. In other words, our approach not only enables the fabrication of individual LM fibers but also establishes a complete LM-based sensing platform. This allows for centralized sensing from single to multiple fibers, thereby broadening their applicability in electronic systems. In response to the reviewer’s comments, we have revised and expanded the manuscript to better emphasize the novelty and originality of our work.

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this critical point regarding process parameters. Their insightful observation demonstrates a deep understanding of materials processing and directly addresses a core aspect of our methodology, the precise control of coating quality. The four parameters highlighted—drawing speed, fiber modulus, ambient temperature, and Galinstan droplet volume—form the foundation for achieving reproducible, high-performance liquid metal coatings. This comment inspired what we consider one of the most valuable aspects of our revision: a full-factorial parametric analysis that has substantially strengthened the scientific contribution of our work.
Guided by the reviewer’s suggestion, we conducted a systematic experimental campaign to examine both the individual and interactive effects of each parameter on coating uniformity, microstructural quality, and interfacial adhesion. Several key insights emerged, refining our processing protocol. Most notably, drawing speed proved to be the dominant factor. At speeds approaching 20 cm/s, the liquid metal–copper reaction becomes kinetically limited, resulting in non-uniform coverage and defective interfaces. This finding enabled us to define a precise operational window for high-speed coating. In contrast, the Young’s modulus of the elastomeric fiber substrate had a surprisingly negligible effect across the tested range, suggesting broad material compatibility for our method. Similarly, the Galinstan droplet volume minimally affected final fiber morphology, provided complete surface wetting was achieved, simplifying process control. Variations within a standard ambient temperature range also had no measurable impact, confirming the robustness of the deposition process under typical laboratory conditions. In response to the comments, we have conducted additional experiments and provided detailed information on the fabrication process as suggested.

This design rationale is grounded in the unique material advantages of liquid metals: their inherent fluidity enables exceptional deformation tolerance, while their metallic nature ensures superior electrical conductivity. Experimental results confirm that the electrode maintains stable electrical performance even under large strain conditions. Unlike strain sensors, which operate based on resistance changes in response to mechanical deformation, our liquid metal electrode is designed specifically for reliable signal transmission. Signal transmission electrodes require minimal resistance variation to ensure signal integrity, whereas strain sensors rely on significant resistance changes for sensitivity detection. Guided by this design principle, we have successfully developed a fiber-shaped electrode that combines high conductivity with outstanding mechanical stability, offering an innovative solution for signal transmission in wearable devices. We believe this clarification helps to better articulate the innovations and potential applications of our work. Rather, our study is centered on the broader application of bioelectrical signal acquisition and regulation. In particular, we utilize the excellent flexibility and conductivity of liquid metal electrodes to achieve high-fidelity recording of electromyography (EMG) and electrocardiography (ECG) signals. Furthermore, to realize stable in vivo electrical stimulation, we incorporate MWCNT/SEBS–PEDOT:PSS inert electrodes as a complementary component.
The core concept underlying our approach is to establish a robust and reliable signal transmission pathway. The liquid metal electrodes, owing to their unique fluidity and mechanical resilience, provide a stable electrical interface even under dynamic strain conditions. In parallel, in regions that may be susceptible to electrochemical corrosion or interfacial instability, the introduction of inert electrodes effectively addresses these challenges. In this manuscript, the authors have demonstrated a multifunctional bioelectronic fiber fabricated by employing an elastomeric core fiber and subsequent layer-by-layer chemical solution deposition processes. Nonetheless, there remain several critical issues and experimental details that should be addressed clearly to make this manuscript suitable for publication in a high-impact journal such as Nature Communications. Therefore, a major revision is recommended.

1. The coating of liquid metals onto yarns with polymeric or metallic surfaces has already been reported in previous studies. (https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.1c05762, https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202105587, https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.9b23083). Therefore, it is essential to clarify and emphasize the distinctive novelty of your approach compared to these prior studies. This differentiation should be explicitly highlighted.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We have carefully studied the suggested literature and recognize that these works indeed demonstrate the successful integration of liquid metal on fabric substrates for various applications. However, it is important to note that these systems achieve their functionality primarily at the fabric or textile level, whereas our research focuses specifically on engineering functional devices at the single-fiber level. This fundamental difference in the scale of the functional unit (fabric vs. single fiber) leads to distinctly different material platforms, fabrication methodologies, and target applications.
Due to their superior flexibility, isotropic deformability, breathability, and lightweight nature, single fiber-based electronics are uniquely advantageous for integration with biological tissues. In this context, liquid metal fibers have attracted growing attention for their outstanding conductivity, intrinsic stretchability, facile phase transition, and the potential to be woven into smart textiles. Nevertheless, current liquid metal single fiber fabrication methods mainly rely on direct coating or injecting LM into hollow or thermoplastic fibers to form LM-core structures (Liquid Metal Fibers. Adv. Fiber Mater. 4, 987–1004 (2022)). These approaches often suffer from uneven coating, relatively large diameters, or poor skin contact of the conductive components. Our study addresses these challenges by introducing a liquid-phase processing strategy for the fabrication of single LM fibers. Unlike large-area thin films or woven fabrics, the processing of individual fibers is inherently more complex. At the microscale, highly uniform electrochemical deposition is required to achieve continuous and stable LM fiber formation. In the revised manuscript, we have further investigated the influence of various fabrication parameters on LM deposition and fiber quality. Moreover, beyond the chemical deposition of LM fibers, we have seamlessly integrated inert electrodes to develop an LM-fiber-based conductive sensing system. In other words, our approach not only enables the fabrication of individual LM fibers but also establishes a complete LM-based sensing platform. This allows for centralized sensing from single to multiple fibers, thereby broadening their applicability in electronic systems.
In response to the reviewer’s comments, we have revised and expanded the manuscript to better emphasize the novelty and originality of our work.

The main challenge arises from the structural differences between films and fibers: large area films possess abundant reactive interfaces that readily interact with liquid metals, whereas single fibers have a much smaller surface area and thus require higher quality electrochemical coatings to achieve uniform and stable encapsulation. To address this issue, we introduced an inert CNT/PEDOT:PSS electrode layer, allowing the exposed regions to directly contact biofluids and perform sensing functions. 2. In the fabrication process of the fiber electrodes, multiple layers (e.g., PDA, AgNP, and Cu) are sequentially deposited. Each layer is expected to significantly influence the mechanical and electrical properties of the fibers. Detailed characterization of changes in fiber diameter, stretchability, and electrical conductivity at each fabrication stage should be provided.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment, which we fully agree with and believe has significantly enhanced the scientific depth of our work through the supplementary analysis it prompted. In comprehensive response to the suggestion, we designed and completed a systematic series of supplementary experiments. By precisely characterizing changes in key fiber parameters before and after deposition of the polydopamine (PDA) adhesion layer, silver nanoparticle (AgNP) activation layer, copper (Cu) conductive layer, and liquid metal layer, we obtained quantitative data on the evolution of diameter distribution, mechanical properties (stress-strain curves), and electrical conductivity. The results clearly demonstrate distinct stage-specific characteristics during the transformation of the fiber from an insulating substrate to a high-performance conductive electrode: the PDA layer primarily enhances interfacial adhesion,the AgNP layer serves mainly to catalyze Cu film formation and does not provide conductivity, the Cu plating significantly improves electrical conductivity, and the liquid metal layer further enhances conductivity. Overall, the construction of each functional layer showed limited impact on mechanical properties. To visually demonstrate this multi-layer fabrication process, we have integrated a summary figure of the key data as a new chart in the revised manuscript. This figure systematically presents the stepwise diameter increase, evolution of stress-strain behavior, and orders-of-magnitude improvement in electrical conductivity, providing direct evidence for understanding the construction mechanism and performance regulation of the multi-layer electrode. We are confident that these supplementary data strongly support the rationality of the multi-layer structural design and further validate the controllability and reproducibility of the process route.

3. The thickness and deposition amount of the internal layers (PDA, AgNW, and Cu layer) could significantly impact the quantity and uniformity of the liquid metal coating. Is there any relevant data available?
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful comment regarding the critical importance of controlling the thickness and quality of the inner functional layers (PDA, AgNP, and Cu) for achieving uniform and complete coating of liquid metal. In response to this valuable suggestion, we conducted a systematic optimization study of the process parameters to elucidate the influence of each functional layer on the final coating quality. Given the difficulty in directly quantifying the deposition amount of each functional layer by weight, we used reaction time as the key control parameter and performed systematic characterization of the fiber surface morphology using high-resolution SEM. This approach allowed us to establish the intrinsic relationship between process parameters, microstructure, and coating performance. Specifically, we investigated the effects of PDA polymerization time (3-14 hours), AgNP deposition time (0.5-3 hours), and Cu electroplating time (5-30 minutes) on the morphological evolution of each corresponding layer and their subsequent impact on the quality of the Galinstan coating. The experimental results demonstrate that a PDA polymerization time of 12 hours leads to the formation of a uniform and continuous adhesion layer, providing an ideal foundation for subsequent metal deposition. AgNP deposition for 3 hours achieves sufficient surface coverage, forming an effective conductive activation layer. Cu electroplating for 20 minutes produces a continuous and dense metal film, serving as an excellent conductive substrate for Galinstan coating. Together, these optimized parameters ensure ideal full-surface coverage by the final liquid metal coating.

A 3-hour AgNP deposition achieved sufficient surface coverage to act as an effective conductive activation layer, while a 30-minute copper electroplating produced a continuous and dense metallic film that served as an excellent conductive substrate for the subsequent Galinstan coating. Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable comment. Since the solution-based process makes it difficult to directly quantify the precise weight of PEDOT:PSS, we therefore conducted a systematic quantitative study focusing on the effect of electrochemical deposition cycles, an important parameter that directly determines the amount and thickness of the functional layer, on the electrochemical performance of the electrodes. Multiple gradients ranging from 0 to 40 deposition cycles were examined. Key parameters, including volumetric capacitance and cathodic charge storage capacity, were systematically characterized as a function of coating cycles, and cyclic voltammetry was employed to compare the electrochemical behavior of electrodes with different deposition numbers in PBS solution. The results revealed a clear saturation effect. When the number of PEDOT:PSS deposition cycles reached 30, the electrochemical capacity of the electrodes plateaued. Based on this saturation phenomenon and comprehensive performance evaluation, we ultimately selected 30 electrochemical deposition cycles of PEDOT:PSS as the optimal process condition. This choice ensures high electrochemical performance while effectively avoiding issues associated with excessive material deposition, such as increased interfacial brittleness and reduced ion diffusion rates.

6. The authors demonstrated several interesting applications, such as textile-based wireless power transmission (inductor coil), ECG, and EMG signal monitoring. Specifically, the electrodes shown in Fig. 5a and Fig. 5g are designed with 2-plied fibers. Was there any signal interference (crosstalk) between the two adjacent fiber electrodes?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. In our design, the encapsulation layer has a thickness of approximately 25 µm, leading to a total thickness of about 50 µm when two layers are stacked. The breakdown strength of SEBS is around 39 MV/m, which means that a 50 µm layer can withstand an electric field of nearly 1950 V. Under direct current (DC) conditions, such insulation thickness is more than sufficient to prevent electrical interference. The situation is inherently more complex under high-frequency alternating current conditions. Crosstalk between adjacent conductors is primarily caused by capacitive and inductive coupling, and with an interline spacing as small as 50 µm, perceptible interference could arise in the MHz range. However, in the context of flexible sensing and electrical stimulation applications, the signals we employ are almost exclusively DC, while the AC components are of very low frequency; in this study, the maximum operating frequency is only 100 Hz. At such low frequencies, capacitive and inductive coupling effects are negligible, and significant interference is therefore unlikely. Consistently, no evidence of crosstalk was observed in our experimental studies.
7. The authors also have presented an intriguing application involving PEDOT:PSS-coated electrodes for neural stimulation. However, PEDOT:PSS is amphiphilic and known to have potential leaching risks in wet physiological environments. Therefore, the authors should evaluate the resistance stability and amount of PEDOT:PSS under prolonged immersion conditions.
Response: The potential leaching of PEDOT:PSS in physiological environments is indeed a critical issue that must be addressed for its applications in bioelectronics. Compared to directly coated PEDOT:PSS films, electrochemically polymerized PEDOT:PSS coatings are generally more compact, exhibit stronger adhesion to the substrate, and contain a lower proportion of hydrophilic sulfonate groups, thereby reducing the likelihood of short-term leakage. To evaluate the stability of our PEDOT:PSS coatings, we conducted an accelerated aging test. Specifically, the fabricated fiber electrodes were continuously immersed in water at 37 °C for 72 hours, and their electrochemical responses in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH = 7.4) were monitored every 12 hours. The PEDOT:PSS layer was deposited onto a robust, hydrophobic, and elastic SEBS/CNT conductive substrate, which may have facilitated strong physical and/or chemical interactions at the interface. The results demonstrated excellent stability of the PEDOT:PSS coatings. As shown in Figure S13, no significant change in interfacial impedance was observed during the 72-hour immersion period.
In the revised manuscript, “To ensure the reliability of the fiber electrodes in physiological environments, we evaluated the long-term stability of the PEDOT:PSS functional layer in simulated body fluid (phosphate-buffered saline, PBS, pH 7.4). Throughout the immersion period, no significant increase or fluctuation in impedance was observed, indicating that the interfacial properties between the coating and the electrolyte remained intact (Fig. S13). ”

Response: We thank the reviewers for their valuable suggestions. To quantitatively assess the mechanical compatibility of the fiber electrodes, we systematically measured their Young’s modulus and linear density (mass per unit length). The results indicate a Young’s modulus of 1.852 MPa and a linear density of 15.79 μg/cm, corresponding to a total mass of 1.579 mg for a 10 cm fiber. Overall, this elastic modulus is on the same order of magnitude as that of neural tissue, slightly higher than the modulus of the nerve. It is noteworthy that similar polymer materials, including the same type of TPU used in this study, have been extensively validated for in vivo implantation and neural stimulation applications (Advanced Functional Materials, 2023, 33(33): 2303134; Neural Networks, 2023, 162: 212-224; Advanced Sensor Research, 2025, 4(7): 2500002; Advanced Healthcare Materials, 2025, 14(3): 2404296), demonstrating that materials with comparable mechanical properties and weight can be safely employed in implantable electronic devices.
